summary: Describes the Cryptographic Message Syntax, used to digitally sign, digest, authenticate or encrypt messages. It was replaced by RFC 3369 and RFC 3370.

eli5.summary: A standard kind of envelope that can be sealed, signed or locked, so whoever receives it knows who sent it and that nobody peeked.

subtitle: A common envelope format for digitally signing, digesting, authenticating or encrypting any message.

tldr.problem: Applications such as secure e-mail need one agreed way to wrap arbitrary data with signatures, message digests, authentication codes or encryption, and to carry the keys and certificates needed to check or open it.
tldr.mechanism: CMS defines a top-level ContentInfo wrapper and six content types (data, signed-data, enveloped-data, digested-data, encrypted-data, authenticated-data), described in ASN.1 and encoded with BER. Wrappers can be nested, so data can be signed and then enveloped.
tldr.outcome: CMS is derived from PKCS #7 version 1.5. RFC 2630 has been obsoleted by RFC 3369 and RFC 3370, so it is a historical stage of the specification.

today: RFC 2630 is a Proposed Standard that has been obsoleted by RFC 3369 and RFC 3370, which are the current definition of CMS. Use those rather than this document.

sections.title: What CMS Is and How It Is Built
sections.content:
The Cryptographic Message Syntax (CMS) is an encapsulation syntax for data protection. It supports digital signatures, message authentication codes and encryption, and it allows multiple encapsulation: one envelope can be nested inside another, and one party can sign data that was already encapsulated. Arbitrary attributes, such as signing time, can be signed along with the content, and others, such as countersignatures, can be attached to a signature.

CMS is derived from PKCS #7 version 1.5 (RFC 2315). Backward compatibility is preserved wherever possible, with changes to carry attribute certificates and to support key agreement. It can work with certificate-based key management architectures such as the one defined by the PKIX working group.

Values are described in ASN.1 and encoded using BER, typically as octet strings. The RFC says it does not address how to encode octet strings for reliable transmission through e-mail systems that cannot carry arbitrary octets.

An implementation that conforms MUST implement the protection content ContentInfo and the data, signed-data and enveloped-data content types. The digested-data, encrypted-data and authenticated-data types are optional.
sections.eli5: CMS is a set of rules for packing a message into protective wrappers. You can stack wrappers, like putting a signed letter inside a locked box.

sections.title: The Outer Wrapper and Content Types
sections.content:
Every CMS object is a ContentInfo: a contentType, which is an object identifier, and the content itself, whose type is determined by the identifier. Other documents may define new content types, whose ASN.1 type should not be a CHOICE.

The six types defined here are:

  • data: arbitrary octet strings such as ASCII text files, with interpretation left to the application. It is generally placed inside one of the other types.
  • signed-data: content plus zero or more signatures.
  • enveloped-data: encrypted content plus encrypted keys for one or more recipients.
  • digested-data: content plus a message digest of it.
  • encrypted-data: encrypted content with no recipients or keys; keys are managed by other means.
  • authenticated-data: content, a message authentication code (MAC) and encrypted authentication keys for recipients.

The design goal is single-pass processing with indefinite-length BER, which helps when content is large, stored on tape or piped from another process. The one exception is that signed attributes and authenticated attributes MUST be DER encoded, so that recipients can verify content carrying attributes they do not recognize.
sections.eli5: Every CMS object has a label saying what kind of wrapper it is, then the wrapper itself. There are six kinds, from a plain note to a signed, locked or checked one.

sections.title: Signed-data
sections.content:
Signed-data holds content of any type and zero or more signatures, and any number of signers can sign in parallel. Building it takes four steps: compute a message digest of the content for each signer with that signer's digest algorithm; sign the digest with the signer's private key; collect the signature and signer details into a SignerInfo; and gather the digest algorithms, the SignerInfo values and the content into a SignedData value, along with certificates and CRLs.

The signer's certificate is named in sid, either by issuer name and serial number or by a subject key identifier. A SignerInfo can carry signedAttrs, which are signed along with the content, and unsignedAttrs. If the content is not of type id-data, signed attributes are required. When present they MUST include a content-type attribute and a message-digest attribute, and then the signature covers the DER encoding of the attributes rather than the content directly.

The eContent may be omitted to make an external signature, where the signed content travels separately. To verify, a recipient recomputes the digest itself and checks it with the signer's public key, and MUST NOT rely on any digest values computed by the originator. Useful attributes include signing time (taken on trust, at the recipient's discretion) and countersignature, an unsigned attribute that signs another signature, so series of countersignatures can be built.
sections.eli5: Signing is like sealing a letter with your personal stamp. The receiver checks the stamp against your known stamp, so they know it is really from you and was not changed.

sections.title: Enveloped-data and Key Management
sections.content:
Enveloped-data keeps content secret. A random content-encryption key is generated, the content is encrypted with it, and the key is encrypted separately for each recipient, giving each recipient a digital envelope. The recipient decrypts the key and then the content. The same algorithm and key are used for all recipients, and recipientInfos comes before the encrypted content so a value can be processed in a single pass.

Each RecipientInfo uses one of three key management techniques, and any mix may be used for recipients of the same content:

  • Key transport (KeyTransRecipientInfo): the content-encryption key is encrypted in the recipient's public key.
  • Key agreement (KeyAgreeRecipientInfo): the recipient's public key and the sender's private key generate a pairwise key, in which the content-encryption key is encrypted. An optional user keying material (UKM) ensures a different key each time.
  • Previously distributed symmetric keys (KEKRecipientInfo): the key is encrypted in a key-encryption key already shared with the recipient.

Some content-encryption algorithms need input that is a multiple of k octets. The RFC then pads with k-(lth mod k) octets, each of that value, and always pads, even when the input is already a multiple of the block size, so the padding can be removed unambiguously. This is well defined only if k is less than 256.
sections.eli5: You lock the message with a random key, then put copies of that key into small boxes, each one locked so only one friend can open it. Every friend opens their own box, gets the key, and reads the message.

sections.title: Digested, Encrypted and Authenticated Data, and Algorithms
sections.content:
Digested-data adds a message digest to content to provide integrity, and its result commonly becomes the input to enveloped-data. Encrypted-data has no recipients; its typical use is encrypting data for local storage, perhaps with a password as the key. Authenticated-data carries a MAC computed with a random message-authentication key, which is encrypted for each recipient using the same RecipientInfo techniques as enveloped-data. Its version shall be 0.

Section 12 lists the algorithms. Implementations MUST include SHA-1 as a digest algorithm and SHOULD include MD5. They MUST include DSA for signatures, and MAY include RSA. For key management they MUST include X9.42 Ephemeral-Static Diffie-Hellman key agreement, and for content encryption they MUST include Triple-DES in CBC mode and SHOULD include RC2 in CBC mode. Key transport with RSA SHOULD be included, and symmetric key-encryption key management is optional. Triple-DES and RC2 key wrap algorithms are specified in section 12.6.

Algorithms are identified by AlgorithmIdentifier values, so new ones can be added without changing the structure.
sections.eli5: The other wrappers do smaller jobs: one attaches a fingerprint so changes can be spotted, one just locks the message with a key you share some other way, and one adds a secret-code check for each receiver.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC lists what implementations MUST protect: the signer's private key (compromise permits masquerade), the key management private key, key-encryption keys and content-encryption keys (compromise may disclose messages), and the message-authentication key (compromise may allow undetectable modification). They MUST randomly generate content-encryption keys, message-authentication keys, initialization vectors and padding, since weak pseudo-random generators can make keys easy to reproduce.

When a key-encryption key and a content-encryption key use different algorithms, the effective security is that of the weaker one. For example, 168-bit Triple-DES content wrapped with a 40-bit RC2 key gives at most 40 bits of protection, so key-encryption algorithms must be as strong or stronger than content-encryption algorithms.

Countersigning can be applied to an inappropriate signature, so implementations should verify the original signature first or countersign only in a context that ensures appropriate signatures. The RFC also warns that RSA encryption as defined in PKCS #1 version 1.5 (RFC 2313) is vulnerable to adaptive chosen ciphertext attacks, which are far less feasible in store-and-forward S/MIME than in interactive protocols. PKCS #1 version 2.0 (RFC 2437) recommends OAEP, and support for it is expected to be added to a future version of CMS. Algorithm implementations should be modular because algorithms become weaker over time.
sections.eli5: Keep your keys safe, make them with real randomness, and do not lock a strong chest with a flimsy lock, because a thief only needs to beat the weakest part.

items.title: Key transport
items.text: Content-encryption key encrypted in the recipient's public key.

items.title: Key agreement
